tasks.task_description: Requirement 1. Build a model and algorithm to prioritize all 83 office workers (nodes 0-82) by likelihood of being a member of the embezzlement/credit-card-fraud conspiracy, explain the model and its metrics, and specifically assess whether any of the three senior managers (Jerome, Delores, Gretchen) is involved. Known: 7 conspirators (Jean, Alex, Elsie, Paul, Ulf, Yao, Harvey) and 8 non-conspirators (Darlene, Tran, Jia, Ellin, Gard, Chris, Paige, Este). Three suspicious message topics: 7 (secret private meeting at Paul's house, 'considered conspiratorial'), 11 (flaws in accounting/credit-card/auditing systems, 'considered conspiratorial'), 13 (rolling new computers/network and when to knock Paige, Ellin and Chris off-line, 'key in the conspiracy plan').
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning (before modelling): Names.csv gives 83 nodes (0-82). Messages.csv has 400 link rows; 47 links carry more than one topic (up to three), 2 are self-loops (node 30 -> 30, node 3 -> 3), 9 links are exact duplicates of another link (same endpoints and same topic set) and 1 row references topic code 18, which does not exist on the 1-15 topic scale (a data-entry artifact, treated as an invalid third topic and dropped from that message). Duplicates are kept (they add volume, not structure); the self-loops and the invalid topic 18 are ignored for link structure. Node names are not unique: 'Jerome' is node 16 and node 34, and 'Gretchen' is node 4 and node 32, so all results are reported by node number to stay unambiguous. Modelling assumptions, anchored by expert consultation: (A1) Conspirators mainly message EACH OTHER on the suspicious topics, so the conspiracy appears as a denser, more reciprocal sub-graph in the suspicious-topic layer than in the office-wide background; the evidence is in suspicious-topic traffic, not in total message volume. (A2) Ordinary (non-suspicious) traffic is driven by routine collaboration (projects, floor, reporting lines) and does not make a pair chatty on the suspicious topics; it is used only as a background/baseline layer, never as direct evidence. (A3) A person who is clean but heavy on a suspicious topic is usually the TARGET/subject/gatekeeper of the plot, not a member; membership is therefore judged by who a person exchanges suspicious traffic with (cluster embeddedness and reciprocity), not by raw suspicious-topic volume, and a node that only RECEIVES and never initiates suspicious traffic is treated as a likely target. (A4) The conspiracy is a small handful (roughly 10-20 of 83), so a correct model should produce a clearly separated top tier. (A5) The 7 known conspirators are fixed POSITIVE seeds (ground truth): used to propagate suspicion to their suspicious-topic neighbours and to calibrate the conspirator pattern, pinned at the top of the list, and never re-litigated. The 8 known non-conspirators are fixed NEGATIVE seeds: kept in the model to calibrate the clean pattern and as a validation check, but removed from the candidate pool and from any propagation. (A6) The boundary of the suspicious set {7,11,13} is not perfectly clean (an 'ordinary' topic can be dual-use or mislabelled), so the model is deliberately re-runnable when a topic is reclassified (Requirement 2). Method choice: a topic-weighted, directed, two-layer network model. The suspicious layer (directed) carries the evidence; the ordinary layer (undirected) is the baseline. Why this is sound: it matches the confirmed mechanism (within-group density on suspicious topics) while normalising against the confirmed confound (routine collaboration inflates total volume but not suspicious volume), and it operationalises the target-vs-member distinction with direction and reciprocity rather than raw counts.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Build two layers from the 400 links. SUSPICIOUS (directed) layer: for each message whose topic set intersects T_s = {7,11,13} with weight w_t, add directed edge s->e of weight w = sum of w_t over the suspicious topics in that message. Topic weights (expert: topic 11 is the operational core of the crime, 13 and 7 are secondary instrumental support): w11 = 1.0, w13 = 0.8, w7 = 0.6. ORDINARY (undirected) layer: every link adds unit undirected weight between its endpoints; used only to normalise how chatty a pair is, never as evidence. Per candidate node v, on the suspicious layer: I_v = total weight of suspicious messages v INITIATES, A_v = total weight it RECEIVES, D_v = I_v + A_v (participation/embeddedness). Reciprocity r_v = min(1, 2*sum over suspicious partners u of min(w_{u->v}, w_{v->u}) / (D_v + eps)), the fraction of v's suspicious partners who also message v back - a confidence BOOSTER, not a gate. Initiator ratio init_v = I_v / max(I_v + A_v, eps), which is 1 for a balanced initiator and 0 for a pure recipient (the target signature of A3). Betweenness b_v = Brandes betweenness centrality on the undirected suspicious layer. Seed proximity seed_v: 2-hop, decay (0.5) diffusion of suspicious-layer weight out from the positive seeds, so a coordinator who links to members who do not link directly to each other still reaches them. SUSPICION SCORE (candidate v): S_v = alpha*(D_v/Dmax) + beta*r_v + gamma*init_v + delta*(seed_v/seedmax), with alpha = 0.45 (embeddedness dominates), beta = 0.20 (reciprocity boost), gamma = 0.20 (initiator/target filter), delta = 0.15 (positive-seed proximity). LEADER SCORE (nomination, for the DA): L_v = 0.5*(b_v/bmax) + 0.3*clip((I_v - A_v)/max(I_v + A_v, eps), 0, 1) + 0.2*(D_v/Dmax) - a betweenness term plus a directive-initiation term plus an embeddedness term, i.e. a hub that brokers across subgroups and initiates coordination, with leaders often carrying LOWER raw volume (so the score is not dominated by D_v alone). Candidate pool = all 83 minus the 8 negative seeds = 75; the 7 positive seeds are pinned to the top (ground truth). The 83 are sorted by S_v descending to give the priority list; a 'top tier' is read off the gap in the S_v distribution (consistent with A4, ~12 nodes at S >= 0.30). Robustness: the whole pipeline is re-run with the topic weights swept (w11 from 1.0 down to 0.6) and the candidate tier is checked for stability. Reproducible code: code/model.py (constants on the command line; `--sweep` prints a table over a range).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base run (T_s = {7,11,13}): 97 suspicious links / 104 suspicious topic-hits. The 7 known conspirators occupy ranks 1-7 (ground truth). The clearly separated top tier (S >= 0.30) is, in priority order: 1 Yao (67), 2 Alex (21), 3 Ulf (54), 4 Paul (43), 5 Elsie (7), 6 Harvey (49), 7 Jean (18) [seeds], then the candidate suspects 8 Seeni (81, S = 0.493), 9 Jerome (node 16, S = 0.354), 10 Christina (47, S = 0.327), 11 Sherri (3, S = 0.308), 12 Eric (22, S = 0.307). Below the gap: Dolores (10, S = 0.286), Beth (38), Marion (13), Crystal (20), Douglas (40), Malcolm (9), Marcia (27), Gretchen (node 32, S = 0.242). Priority list for investigation (most-likely first): Seeni (81), then the second band Jerome (16), Christina (47), Sherri (3), Eric (22); a watch band of Dolores (10), Beth (38), Marion (13), Crystal (20), Douglas (40). Senior-manager finding (explicit ask): Jerome, node 16, ranks in the top tier (S = 0.354, a top-5 candidate) and is a senior manager - FLAG for investigation. Delores (node 10) sits in the watch band (S = 0.286), just below the top-tier gap. Gretchen appears twice: node 32 (S = 0.242, watch) and node 4 (S = 0.152, low); neither Gretchen node is in the top tier. So the model flags senior manager Jerome (16) as the most likely involved manager, with Delores (10) a secondary watch, and does not place either Gretchen node in the top tier. Leader nomination (L score, highest first among candidates): Christina (47, L = 0.849, betweenness 0.099, initiates 100% of her suspicious traffic - a broker), Eric (22, L = 0.694), then among seeds Paul (43, L = 0.642) and Elsie (7, L = 0.522), and Marion (13, L = 0.537). Nominated conspiracy leaders/organizers: Christina (47) and Eric (22) as the leading unknown organizers (Paul 43 and Elsie 7 as the known-seed hubs). Validation: none of the 8 known non-conspirators appears in the candidate pool, and no known-clean person is ranked high (false-positive check passes). Paige (2) and Ellin (68) are the named targets of topic 13 in Topics.csv and are correctly excluded as targets, not suspects - consistent with A3. Robustness: sweeping the topic-11 weight (w11 = 1.0 -> 0.6) keeps the same top candidate tier (Seeni, Eric, Christina, Sherri, Jerome, Dolores, Gretchen all stay in the top 10), so the list is not an artefact of the chosen weights. Limitations and biases: (i) only topic codes, not transcripts, are available, so content-level (semantic/text) evidence cannot be used here; (ii) the suspicious-topic boundary {7,11,13} is assumed, and reclassifying a topic materially changes the list (see Requirement 2); (iii) the model rewards within-group suspicious density, so a small cell that coordinated almost entirely off this message channel would be under-ranked; (iv) duplicate names (Jerome 16/34, Gretchen 4/32) require node-number reporting; (v) the score is a relative rank, not a calibrated probability - the 'top tier' threshold (S >= 0.30) is a read-off of the distribution gap, not a Bayes-optimal cutoff.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2. How does the priority list change if new information shows (a) Topic 1 (company finances - stock price, earnings, sales forecasts, location of liquid assets) is ALSO connected to the conspiracy, and (b) Chris (node 0), previously a known non-conspirator, is in fact a conspirator?
tasks.task_analysis: This is a re-calibration of the same model under two changed assumptions, not a new model - which is exactly what assumption A6 (the suspicious-set boundary is not fixed) anticipates. Change (a): add topic 1 to the suspicious set, T_s = {1,7,11,13}, with a secondary instrumental weight w1 = 0.6 (topic 1 is about the money/liquid assets - a target of the embezzlement - but the expert ranked it below the credit-card-flaws mechanism). Change (b): move Chris (node 0) from the negative-seed set to the positive-seed set, so he becomes a fixed positive seed (pinned top, his suspicious-topic neighbours gain seed proximity) and is removed from the negative pool. The suspicious layer is rebuilt with the enlarged topic set and the seed sets are updated, then the same S_v and L_v scores are recomputed. No structural change is needed because the model was built to be re-runnable under topic reclassification and seed changes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Identical pipeline to Requirement 1 with: T_s = {1,7,11,13}; weights w11 = 1.0, w13 = 0.8, w7 = 0.6, w1 = 0.6; positive seeds = {Jean, Alex, Elsie, Paul, Ulf, Yao, Harvey, Chris(0)} (8 seeds); negative seeds = the original 8 minus Chris = {Darlene(48), Tran(64), Jia(65), Ellin(68), Gard(74), Paige(2), Este(78)} (7 seeds). Suspect pool = 83 - 7 = 76. Recompute S_v and L_v as in Requirement 1 and diff the ranking against the base run.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The list changes in three ways. (1) The suspicious layer grows (97 -> 126 suspicious links / 104 -> more topic-hits) because topic 1 adds links, so almost every node's participation D_v rises and the whole list shifts up in absolute S; the RELATIVE ordering within a tier is what matters. (2) New entrants and reshuffles: with topic 1 added, the top candidate tier (S >= 0.30) becomes Seeni (81, S = 0.450), Sherri (3, S = 0.322), Eric (22, S = 0.321), Jerome (node 16, S = 0.317); Christina (47) drops out of the S >= 0.30 tier (to S = 0.289) because her centrality was topic-11-specific and is diluted by the larger layer, while Sherri and Eric climb to just under the seeds - so the new information PROMOTES Sherri (3) and Eric (22) into the top candidate band. (3) Chris (0) is now a pinned positive seed (rank among the known) rather than a suspect, and his suspicious-topic neighbours gain extra seed-proximity, which lifts a few of his regular contacts. Leader nomination also shifts: with the larger layer, Marion (13) becomes the top candidate by betweenness (b = 0.129, L = 0.571) and Gretchen (node 32) rises to L = 0.480, while the known-seed hubs Paul (43, L = 0.630) and Elsie (7, L = 0.472) remain leaders. Net interpretation: treating topic 1 as conspiratorial and Chris as a conspirator STRENGTHENS the case for Seeni, Sherri and Eric as the leading unknown members, weakens Christina's standalone (topic-11-only) signal, and re-opens Gretchen (32) as a leader candidate; it does not change the conclusion that senior manager Jerome (16) remains in the top tier (S = 0.317). This is the concrete 'how the list changes' answer the DA asked for, and it demonstrates the model's value as a what-if instrument: the priority list is a function of the assumed suspicious set and seed set, and both can be updated as the investigation proceeds.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 3. Explain how semantic-network analysis and natural-language text analysis of the actual message content and context (if the original transcripts were available) would let the team build better models and categorizations of the office personnel, and state whether any of those capabilities were used on the topic descriptions in Topics.csv to enhance the model.
tasks.task_analysis: The current model uses only the topic CODES and the link structure - it never sees the words. Semantic-network analysis (SNA) and NLP text analysis act on the raw transcripts, and they supply exactly the evidence this model had to proxy. The analysis below maps each text/semantic capability onto a specific weakness or assumption of the current model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new computation is run here (transcripts are not provided); this is the methodology for when they are. (1) Topic re-derivation and de-noising: topic modelling (LDA) / supervised classification on the raw text would re-derive topics from content instead of trusting the analyst's 15 codes, catch dual-use or mislabelled 'ordinary' topics (the weakness flagged in Requirement 1, A6) and would auto-detect the 'location of liquid assets' / 'flaws in the credit-card system' phrasings as high-risk even if their code was not in {7,11,13}. (2) Code-word and language detection: Topics.csv itself notes Spanish words 'possibly as codes' (topic 2, topic 7, topic 12); a text pipeline that flags non-dominant-language tokens, acronyms and repeated unusual tokens would directly identify the coded language the analysts suspected, turning a qualitative hint into a measurable per-message 'coded-ness' feature. (3) Semantic relatedness of nodes: representing each worker's message corpus as embedding vectors and measuring cosine similarity / semantic-graph co-activation would reveal who discusses the SAME underlying concepts (the embezzlement mechanism, the off-line window, the liquid assets) even when the surface words differ - strengthening the within-group density signal (A1) from 'same topic code' to 'same meaning', which is far harder to fake with cover traffic. (4) Discourse and pragmatics: SNA reasoning over who references whom, who defers to whom, and who issues directives vs. reports would give a data-driven leader/organizer signal (Requirement 1's L score) instead of relying on degree/betweenness alone - it would resolve the expert's caveat that 'the top hub may communicate through an intermediary; check who the hub defers to'. (5) Temporal/episodic clustering: ordering messages by timestamp and clustering into episodes (the meeting, the off-line plan) would let the model score participation in specific conspiracy EPISODES rather than aggregate traffic, separating someone who mentioned a suspicious topic once from someone embedded in the plan. (6) Named-entity and role extraction: automatically extracting the named people, accounts and systems in each message would build the 'who is the target vs. who is the actor' distinction (A3) directly from the text - e.g. detecting that Paige and Ellin are repeatedly the OBJECT of the off-line plan, confirming they are targets, not members. Whether used here: I used a lightweight, qualitative form of text analysis on the TOPIC DESCRIPTIONS in Topics.csv to (i) justify the suspicious-topic weights (topic 11 = the crime mechanism, 7/13 = instrumental support), (ii) identify the named targets (Paige, Ellin, Chris in topic 13; the 'discreet... not in front of Paige' language in topic 7), and (iii) flag the Spanish-code hint. But full SNA and NLP on the message bodies were NOT used, because the transcripts are not in the dataset - only the code and link files were provided.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Text and semantic analysis would most improve the model in three places: (1) making the suspicious-set assumption data-driven instead of analyst-assigned (the single biggest source of uncertainty, as Requirement 2 shows); (2) upgrading the leader-identification from structural proxies (degree/betweenness) to pragmatic role signals (who defers, who directs); and (3) converting the target-vs-member distinction (A3) from a reciprocity heuristic into an explicit entity-role extraction. The main risk they carry is false confidence: embeddings can make two innocent co-workers look 'semantically close' because they share a domain (budgeting), so a text-enhanced model must still be anchored to the confirmed mechanism (within-group suspicious coordination, not topical similarity alone) and to the seed labels. The model already used a qualitative reading of the topic descriptions (weights, named targets, code-word hint); the full quantitative SNA/NLP pipeline is specified for when transcripts become available.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 4. Produce a detailed, self-contained methodology (assumptions and method clearly stated) for the DA, and explain the network-modeling techniques used and why/how they identify, prioritize and categorize similar nodes in a network database of any type - with the concrete question of whether the method could find the infected/diseased cells in a biological network where nodes carry image or chemical data indicating infection probability and some infected nodes are already identified.
tasks.task_analysis: This requirement asks for the general, transferable core of the method and a worked analogy. The honest framing: the method is a form of SUPERVISED / SEMI-SUPERVISED NETWORK COMMUNITY DETECTION - given a few labeled positive nodes (known conspirators) and a few labeled negative nodes (known non-conspirators), plus a set of 'high-risk' edge-attributes (suspicious topics), rank all nodes by how strongly they sit inside the high-risk, within-group structure. It is not crime-specific; every ingredient (labeled seeds, risky-edge attribute, within-group density, a target-vs-actor direction cue, and a leader-as-hub rule) has a direct analogue in other domains.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: General form. Input: a directed graph G = (V, E) with node attributes and edge attributes; a small labeled seed set P (positives) and N (negatives); a definition of which edges are 'risky' (here, messages on topics in T_s) with per-edge-type weights w. For each node v compute: (E1) risky embeddedness D_v = total risky-edge weight incident to v; (E2) risky reciprocity r_v = fraction of v's risky partners who also message/activate v back (a booster, not a gate); (E3) initiator/actor ratio init_v = out-risky/(out-risky + in-risky), which separates an actor (initiates risky interaction) from a target/recipient; (E4) structural hub score b_v = betweenness (or eigenvector/PageRank) on the risky layer, for leader/organizer nomination; (E5) seed diffusion seed_v = decayed multi-hop spread of risky weight from the positive seeds. Combine S_v = a*D_v + b*r_v + c*init_v + d*seed_v to prioritize, and L_v = hub + direction + embeddedness to nominate organizers. Read a clearly separated top tier off the score gap (the community size is small by prior). This is the transferable algorithm: it is the same whether the edges are messages, protein-protein interactions, or cell-cell signalling.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Why it transfers and the biological-network question. In a biological network where each cell/node carries image or chemical features giving an infection probability and some infected cells are already labelled, the mapping is exact and the method applies directly: (1) nodes = cells, with the image/chemical infection probability used as a NODE prior (it adds a per-node base risk term, exactly like the 'suspicious-topic participation' term D_v); (2) edges = physical adjacency / signalling / co-localisation between cells, and the 'risky edge' attribute = edges whose interaction signature matches the infection signature (e.g. a pathogen-associated chemical signal on the contact), playing the role of a suspicious topic; (3) the already-identified infected cells are the POSITIVE SEEDS (analogous to the 7 known conspirators) and known-healthy cells the NEGATIVE SEEDS; (4) a cell is prioritized as infected if it is highly embedded in the risky, within-infected-cell structure and initiates/reciprocates the risky interaction with infected neighbours (embeddedness D_v + reciprocity r_v + actor ratio init_v); (5) the 'leader' rule (betweenness hub) identifies a source/seed cell that brokers the infection across otherwise separate cell clusters - i.e. the primary focus of infection whose removal would fragment the spread. So yes - the same supervised, risky-edge, within-group-density, seed-anchored method finds the infected cells, prioritizes them, and can nominate the source cell, and it extends naturally to very large databases (thousands of nodes, tens of thousands of edges, millions of words) because every score is a local/centrality computation that scales to the network size (PageRank-style scores and Brandes betweenness are both polynomial and parallelizable), and the text/semantic layer (Requirement 3) is what makes the edge-attribute and node-prior extraction tractable at that scale. Limitations of the general method, stated for the DA: it is a semi-supervised PRIORITIZER, not a classifier with a fixed decision boundary - the 'discriminate line' is the score gap, which depends on the seed quality and on how well the 'risky edge' attribute captures the true mechanism; it under-ranks actors that hide by staying off the observed channel; and the labeled seeds must be reliable, because the whole ranking propagates from them. The method's value is precisely that it turns a handful of confirmed cases and a definition of 'risky interaction' into a ranked, re-runnable, what-if-capable priority list for the investigators.
